reason: The support cells have membrane sheets that appear suited to insulating the motor neuron fibers, matching the goal.
expectation: The support cells will insulate the motor neuron fibers.

effect: The motor fibers and support cells formed motor nerves, completing the insulation goal; the next goal is to connect sight to muscle commands.
reaction: The segmented wrapping and gaps are an interesting detail about how support cells help signals travel.
reason: Light reflected from the glass should be detected by the eyes, starting the sight pathway.
expectation: The eyes will detect the reflected light and send sensory information along their nerves.

effect: The eyes and reflected light formed a visual information route; it still needs to connect to the nervous system to support muscle commands.
reaction: The change from light rays to a nerve signal makes the first part of the pathway clear.
reason: The sensory route leads toward a central connection, so the central nervous system is the natural next link.
expectation: The visual information route will connect to the central nervous system.

effect: The visual route now connects to the brain, creating a seeing control system that can locate the glass.
reaction: The distinction between locating the target and producing movement is clear.
reason: Motor nerves appear to be the outgoing link needed to turn the seeing system’s information into muscle commands.
expectation: The motor nerves will connect the seeing control system to an outgoing command pathway.

effect: The motor nerves now extend from the control system, but their muscle endings are still unattached.
reaction: The picture makes the remaining connection clear.
reason: The outgoing nerve endings need to connect to the arm muscles to complete the command pathway.
expectation: The motor nerve endings will connect to the arm muscles.

effect: The outgoing nerves connected the control system to the arm, completing the sight-to-command pathway. The next goal is to add information about arm position.
reaction: The inward and outward arrows make the two directions of communication clear.
reason: The stretch receptors are positioned among muscle fibers, so muscle-length changes should activate them.
expectation: The receptors will detect the length change and provide a sensory signal about the arm’s position.

effect: The muscle-length change and stretch receptors formed a position information route that leads toward the central nervous system.
reaction: The two poses make the connection between muscle stretch and sensory information clear.
reason: The guided arm already includes the central nervous system, so connecting the position route should bring that information back to it.
expectation: The sensory route will connect to the guided arm’s central nervous system, completing the position-information pathway.

effect: The position route connected to the arm’s central nervous system, completing the chapter and showing how muscle sensors can provide feedback when the eyes are closed.
reaction: The eyes-closed inset ties the result back to the opening example in a satisfying way.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the position information route to the guided arm was most worthwhile because it completed a pathway I could relate to sensing my own arm without looking.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding the outgoing nerves and then attaching them to the arm felt somewhat predictable, although the separate steps made the pathway clear.

surprise.text: The segmented wrapping, with gaps between support cells, added a detail I had not expected from the initial items.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary. The item pictures and goals gave each connection a recognizable purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: building the sensory and motor pathways made me curious how the remaining body systems would support the arm’s work.
